title: When would you choose EF Core, Dapper or raw SQL?
description: Compare EF Core, Dapper, and raw SQL across productivity, performance, control, and maintainability to make the right data-access choice.

data.text: Choosing a data-access strategy is one of the most frequent architectural decisions in .NET backends. EF Core, Dapper, and raw ADO.NET each occupy a distinct point on the spectrum from developer productivity to raw control. The right choice depends on query complexity, performance requirements, and team expertise.

The common mistake is choosing based on familiarity alone. Some teams reach for EF Core on every project because it is familiar, then suffer N+1 query problems at scale. Others reach for raw SQL everywhere and spend months maintaining hand-written mapping code. The best teams make an intentional choice per bounded context.

data.title: EF Core vs Dapper vs raw SQL

cards.title: EF Core
cards.description: Full-featured ORM with change tracking, LINQ queries, migrations, and lazy/eager loading.
pros: Rapid development with LINQ and migrations
cons: Hidden SQL can surprise you in production
N+1 query risk with lazy loading

cards.title: Dapper
cards.description: Micro-ORM that maps query results to objects with minimal overhead. You write SQL; Dapper hydrates objects.
pros: Explicit queries are easy to audit
Works well with existing stored procedures
cons: Manual object mapping for complex graphs
Requires SQL knowledge from every team member

cards.title: Raw ADO.NET
cards.description: Direct use of SqlConnection, SqlCommand, and SqlDataReader for complete control.
pros: Full control over execution plans and batching

items: Choose EF Core for CRUD-heavy domain logic where productivity matters more than squeezing every millisecond. It excels in internal tools, admin panels, and prototypes where time-to-market is the priority.
Choose Dapper for read-heavy APIs, reporting queries, and stored-procedure integration. Dapper shines when you know the SQL you want and just need fast, reliable hydration.
Choose raw ADO.NET only for extreme-performance paths or when you need precise control over batching, bulk operations, or connection lifecycle that higher-level abstractions cannot express.

data.text: Production systems rarely stick to one tool. A common hybrid is EF Core for the write side (commands and transactions) and Dapper for the read side (queries and projections). This gives you change tracking where you need it and raw SQL performance where queries are complex.

data.title: C#: Dapper query with multi-mapping

items: Using EF Core for large reporting queries that return thousands of rows — use Dapper or a dedicated read model instead.
Using Dapper everywhere just to avoid learning EF Core — you lose migrations, change tracking, and team velocity.
Mixing raw SQL strings without parameters — always parameterize to prevent SQL injection.
Ignoring async — both EF Core and Dapper have async APIs; use them in ASP.NET Core.

data.title: EF Core performance traps
data.text: Enable logging during development to see the SQL EF Core generates. Common traps: Include() loading entire graphs when you only need one field, and AsNoTracking() omission on read-only queries causing unnecessary change-tracker overhead.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: EF Core is best for productivity-heavy write paths and standard CRUD operations.
Dapper is best for read-heavy performance paths and complex reporting queries.
Raw SQL is best reserved for extreme control or bulk operations that abstractions cannot express well.
Hybrid EF Core + Dapper is the most common production pattern.
data.takeaway: Choose your data-access tool based on the query profile, not the framework you know best.
